newsitem.title: LEBANON: Lebanon government, opposition head to showdown.
newsitem.headline: Lebanon government, opposition head to showdown.

text.p: Prime Minister Rafiki al-Hariri's new government headed for a showdown with Lebanon's labour unions and opposition groups on Thursday as troops deployed in Beirut to prevent outlawed demonstrations
Troops started moving in a few hours before Hariri's easy success in a parliamentary vote of confidence on Wednesday night.
Armoured personnel carriers could be heard rumbling through West Beirut late into the night. Truckloads of troops set up checkpoints or patrolled main streets.
Interior Minister Michel al-Murr said demonstrations were banned and the army and security forces would keep order during a general strike planned on Thursday.
Similar protests were aborted in February when the army imposed a nationwide curfew.
A government order on Wednesday night told Beirutis to stay off roads leading to the demonstrators' mustering point and to three other areas the protesters plan to march through.
Opposition groups, labour unions, students and media workers called Thursday's strike and demonstrations last week to demand cancellation of a ban on demonstrations imposed in 1993.

They are also protesting against the government's policies, which they say have failed to give most Lebanese a better life, and against its decision to close scores of private television and radio stations this week, muzzling the opposition.

Hariri, a billionaire leading Lebanon's revival from the 1975-90 civil war, and members of his 25-member cabinet listened patiently in parliament over the past three days as MPs took turns criticising their news statement of aims.
But despite the attacks, 121 MPs present in the 128-seat house voted 102-19 for a new government.
Some deputies said Hariri, in office for four years, cared nothing for the poor and had mired the country in debt to fund big reconstruction projects.
Hariri, replied that things had improved dramatically since he came to power in October, 1992, and 130,000 new jobs had been created.
He said gross domestic product doubles to $11 billion from about $5.5 billion and foreign exchange reserves rose ten-fold.
"It is not true that the government was building bridges and forgetting about people in the past four years," Hariri said.
